summary: Defines OSPF extensions for advertising attributes of the individual member links of a Layer 2 bundle when OSPF runs over the bundle. This lets outside systems control traffic on specific physical links within the bundle.

eli5.summary: A big road with several lanes looks like one road to the map. This lets the map describe each lane separately.

questions: how to advertise link bundle members in ospf
what is an ospf l2 bundle member
how to advertise lag member links in ospf
what is the l2 bundle member attributes sub-tlv
subtitle: How OSPF can tell outside systems about the individual physical links inside a Layer 2 bundle, without changing how routes are computed.

tldr.problem: When OSPF runs over a Layer 2 bundle such as a LAG, it sees one link, so external systems like a Path Computation Element cannot learn about or steer traffic onto individual member links.
tldr.mechanism: A new L2 Bundle Member Attributes sub-TLV (type 24 in OSPFv2, 29 in OSPFv3) carries a 4-octet member descriptor plus nested sub-TLVs with that member's link attributes, such as Adj-SIDs.
tldr.outcome: The information is meant for external entities and does not change OSPF route computation. It can also be passed on through BGP-LS, and it is off by default.

today: RFC 9356 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2023. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 9085 to cover OSPF advertisement into BGP-LS.

sections.title: Why Bundle Members Need Advertising
sections.content:
Sometimes the Layer 3 interface carrying an OSPF adjacency is a Layer 2 bundle, for example a Link Aggregation Group (LAG). That reduces the number of adjacencies OSPF must maintain when there are parallel links between neighbors. But entities outside OSPF, such as Path Computation Elements (PCEs), may want to control traffic on individual member links, and for that they need attribute information for each member.

This document defines sub-TLVs to advertise that information. Similar capabilities were introduced for IS-IS in RFC 8668. It also lets the Adjacency Segment Identifier (Adj-SID) of RFC 8665 and RFC 8666 be advertised per member link, so traffic can be steered over that specific member.
sections.eli5: When many wires are tied together, the router sees one fat cable. Helpers outside the router may want to pick one wire, so each wire needs its own description.

sections.title: What Is and Is Not Covered
sections.content:
The advertisements are for entities external to OSPF and do not alter or change OSPF route computation. The RFC deliberately leaves out several things:

  • which link attributes get advertised, since that depends on the external entities
  • a minimum or default set of attributes
  • how the attributes are configured
  • how the advertisements are used and what impact they have on traffic
  • how the advertisements are passed to external entities
sections.eli5: This RFC only says how to describe each wire. It does not say who reads the description or what they do with it.

sections.title: The L2 Bundle Member Attributes Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The new L2 Bundle Member Attributes sub-TLV works in both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3. In OSPFv2 it is an optional sub-TLV of the Extended Link TLV in the Extended Link Opaque LSA (RFC 7684). In OSPFv3 it is an optional sub-TLV of the Router-Link TLV of the E-Router-LSA (RFC 8362).

It has a Type (24 for OSPFv2, 29 for OSPFv3), a Length covering the value including nested sub-TLVs, a 4-octet L2 Bundle Member Descriptor, and then the member link attribute sub-TLVs. The descriptor is a link-local identifier for the member link, as in RFC 4202 and as the Local Interface ID in RFC 8510.

Including a member means that it is part of the bundle and operationally up. So a router MUST NOT advertise a member that is operationally down or no longer in the bundle. The advertisement may be asymmetric, made by the router on only one end of the link.
sections.eli5: Each wire gets a name tag number, followed by a list of facts about that wire. Only working wires in the bundle get listed.

sections.title: Which Attributes Apply to Members
sections.content:
The nested sub-TLVs come from the sub-TLV space of the parent TLV. Not all make sense per member. Typically, attributes with Layer 3 semantics do not apply, but Layer 2 attributes do. Tables in the RFC list each existing sub-TLV as Y (MAY appear), N (MUST NOT appear) or, for OSPFv3, X (not a Router-Link sub-TLV, so MUST NOT appear).

Examples marked as allowed include Adj-SID, LAN Adj-SID, Shared Risk Link Group, the unidirectional delay, loss and bandwidth sub-TLVs, Administrative Group, TE Metric and Maximum Link Bandwidth. Not allowed are, for instance, SID/Label, Graceful-Link-Shutdown, the Link MSD, Remote IPv4 Address and the L2 Bundle Member Attributes sub-TLV itself.

An implementation MUST ignore any received sub-TLV that is not applicable. Future specifications that add sub-TLVs to the Extended Link TLV or Router-Link TLV MUST state whether they apply to the L2 Bundle Member Attributes sub-TLV.
sections.eli5: Some facts make sense for one wire, like how fast it is. Others only make sense for the whole cable. The RFC has a checklist saying which is which.

sections.title: Passing It On via BGP-LS
sections.content: BGP Link State (BGP-LS, RFC 7752) was extended in RFC 9085 to advertise L2 bundle members and their attributes, but that covered only IS-IS. This document updates RFC 9085 so the OSPF sub-TLV can be advertised into BGP-LS in the same way as described for IS-IS in Section 2.2.3 of that RFC.
sections.eli5: Another system collects maps from many routers. This lets it also collect the wire-by-wire details from routers that speak OSPF.

sections.title: Operations and IANA
sections.content:
Implementations MUST NOT enable the advertisement of L2 bundle members by default, and MUST provide a configuration option to enable it on specific links. The base YANG model for OSPF is RFC 9129, and the configuration for this feature is expected to be added as an augmentation of it.

IANA allocated value 24 in the OSPFv2 Extended Link TLV Sub-TLVs registry and value 29 in the OSPFv3 Extended-LSA Sub-TLVs registry. It also added an L2BM column to both registries to record applicability, and future allocations must say whether the new sub-TLV applies.
sections.eli5: The feature starts switched off. A network operator turns it on for just the cables where it is needed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The advertisements are identical to existing link attribute advertisements, such as those in RFC 3630, RFC 7471, RFC 8665 and RFC 8666, but they are associated with member links of a bundle. The RFC concludes that the security considerations of those documents apply and that no new security issues are introduced.

As always, an environment where unauthorized access to the physical links carrying OSPF occurs allows attacks. The RFC recommends the authentication mechanisms of RFC 5709, RFC 7474, RFC 4552 and RFC 7166 to prevent them.
sections.eli5: Describing each wire adds no new way to cheat. The usual locks on OSPF still apply.

fields.desc: Octets in the value, including nested sub-TLVs.

fields.name: L2 Bundle Member Descriptor
fields.desc: A 4-octet link-local identifier for the member link.
